summary: Lists what a standard way of exporting measured IP traffic flow information from routers, measurement probes, and middleboxes needs to do. It is a requirements memo, not a protocol, and fed into the IPFIX working group's later design work.

eli5.summary: Before building a machine that counts cars on a road and reports the counts, you first write down what the report must say. This memo is that list, for network traffic.

questions: what is ip flow information export
subtitle: A checklist of what a standard way to report measured IP traffic flows must be able to do.

tldr.problem: Routers, probes and middleboxes can measure IP traffic as flows, but every vendor reported those measurements in its own way, so applications on other devices could not rely on a common format.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines flow-related terms, picks five target applications, and derives from them what the metering process, the exporting process and the data transfer must, should or may do.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements memo, not a protocol. It was written as input to the standardization of the IPFIX protocol specifications.

today: RFC 3917 is an Informational RFC, published in October 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the requirements that fed the IPFIX work; its sibling documents are RFC 3955, which evaluates candidate protocols against it, and RFC 3954, which documents NetFlow version 9.

sections.title: Why Flow Export Needs Requirements
sections.content:
Several applications need flow-based IP traffic measurements. The measuring can be done by a router while it forwards traffic, by a middlebox, or by a traffic measurement probe attached to a line or a monitored port. RFC 3917 defines requirements for getting that flow information out of those boxes so that applications on other devices can process it.

The requirements serve as input to the standardization of the IPFIX protocol specifications. Because flow export needs a system of cooperating processes and not just a protocol, the working group specified what each process must do. The memo writes must, may and should in lower case to show that implementors have some freedom in how they meet a requirement. The later information model and protocol documents were to use uppercase keywords as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Lots of gadgets can count network traffic, but each one reports it in its own style. This memo lists what any shared reporting style has to cover.

sections.title: Flows and the Processes Around Them
sections.content:
A flow is a set of IP packets passing an observation point during a certain time interval. All packets in a flow share a set of common properties, which come from packet header fields, from characteristics of the packet itself, or from how the packet was treated (for example the output interface). A flow can be as broad as every packet seen at an interface or as narrow as a single packet.

Four roles are defined. The observation point is a place where packets can be seen, such as a line, a router port or a set of interfaces. The metering process generates flow records through packet header capturing, timestamping, sampling, classifying and maintaining flow records. The exporting process sends flow records to one or more collecting processes. The collecting process receives them; what it does afterwards is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A flow is a group of packets that look alike, like all the letters going from one house to another. One part counts the letters, one part sends the counts, and one part receives them.

sections.title: The Applications Behind the Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements are derived from five applications that the memo considers significant: usage-based accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, attack and intrusion detection, and QoS monitoring. An appendix table shows which requirement comes from which application.

The applications differ in what they demand. Usage-based accounting needs the highest reliability, and the memo states that its own reliability requirements are not sufficient for many accounting systems; RFC 2975 covers accounting needs. Traffic profiling needs a flexible measurement set-up. QoS monitoring often needs clocks synchronized across observation points, but this memo only covers per-flow summaries, so something like jitter measurement, which needs every packet's timestamp, is not fully covered.
sections.eli5: Different people want traffic reports for different jobs: sending bills, planning roads, spotting trouble. The list of rules is built from what all those jobs need.

sections.title: Distinguishing Flows and Metering
sections.content:
Packets with common properties go into the same flow, and one differing property puts a packet into a different flow. The metering process must be able, through configuration, to separate flows by incoming or outgoing interface, source and destination IP address (full match and prefix match), protocol type, and TCP or UDP port numbers. It should do so for the IP version and for SCTP ports. If MPLS or DiffServ is supported at the observation point, it must also separate flows by MPLS label or DiffServ Code Point.

The metering process must be either reliable or known to be unreliable, and it must be able to detect and report that not all packets could be metered. It may support sampling. If the sampling configuration or the overload behavior changes, the affected flow records must be terminated and exported separately, never merged with the new ones. It must generate timestamps for the first and last packet of a flow with at least one-centisecond resolution, allow synchronization with UTC, and detect flow expiration after a timeout.
sections.eli5: The counter must be able to sort packets into piles by who sent them, who gets them and what kind they are. If it changes how it counts, it must start fresh piles and say so.

sections.title: Exporting, Configuring and Special Devices
sections.content:
The exporting process must be able to report a long list of attributes per flow, including the IP version where applicable, source and destination addresses, protocol, ports, a packet counter, a byte counter, the first and last packet timestamps and identifiers for the observation point and the exporting process. Others are only should or may, such as ICMP type and code, interface indexes, TTL and BGP autonomous system numbers. The data model must be extensible and flexible about which attributes a record carries.

For transfer, a congestion-aware protocol must be supported. Loss of flow records must be indicated at the collector so it can gauge how many were lost, and the transfer must be open to extensions such as retransmission, fail-over and acknowledgements, with exponential backoff for retransmission. Confidentiality, integrity and authenticity of the data must be ensured. Push mode reporting is required; pull mode is optional. Anonymization is optional because no standardized method exists.

The memo also lists general requirements: openness to future technologies, support for data collection from hundreds of exporting processes, and duplicate detection when one exporter feeds several collectors. It avoids constraining device architecture and sketches probes, routers, protocol converters, concentrators and proxies.
sections.eli5: The report must say who talked to whom and how much. It must travel safely, without flooding the network, and the receiver must be able to tell if some pages went missing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An IPFIX protocol must be able to carry data over the public Internet, so an attacker may capture, modify or insert packets. The memo names three hazards. First, disclosure: flow records reveal active flows, communication endpoints and traffic patterns, which can be used to spy on users or plan attacks. Encryption and anonymization address this.

Second, forgery: records used for accounting or security could be altered or injected, for example to save money or to hide an attack, or to trick a security application into concluding a DoS attack is under way. Authentication and integrity are required against this. Third, denial of service: a collecting process always expects data and can be flooded, and an exporting process can be a target if it supports pull mode.
sections.eli5: Anyone who reads the traffic report learns who is talking to whom, and anyone who fakes it can fool the people reading it. So the report must be secret and must prove who sent it.

items.title: Usage-based accounting
items.text: Accounting by time or volume, per user, service or class, as input to billing.

items.title: Traffic profiling
items.text: Characterizing flows by duration, volume, time and burstiness.

items.title: Traffic engineering
items.text: Measuring and controlling a network to optimize resource use.

items.title: Attack and intrusion detection
items.text: Spotting unusual or suspicious flows and gathering data for defense.

items.title: QoS monitoring
items.text: Passive measurement of quality parameters for existing traffic.
